newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu ends first 100 days with test by fire.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu ends first 100 days with test by fire.

text.p: Tested by fire, Benjamin Netanyahu has ended his first 100 days as Israel's prime minister by rushing to Washington to try to put out new flames of Palestinian fury.
The right-wing Israeli leader insists his initial three months in office, during which he met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat after expressing reluctance to do so, show he is a peacemaker.

Palestinians accuse him of foot-dragging by failing to implement peace deals they signed with the previous Labour-led government, especially an Israeli promise to pull troops out of many parts of the West Bank city of Hebron.

The West Bank, Gaza Strip and Arab East Jerusalem erupted in four days of rage last week after Netanyahu, in what he called an expression of Jewish sovereignty over all of the holy city, opened an archaeological tunnel near Moslem shrines.
Fifty-seven Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in the worst Israeli-Palestinian violence since a framework peace deal was signed in 1993.

Netanyahu, vowing Arafat would reap no political gain from bloodshed he accused the Palestinian leader of instigating, sent tanks to the edges of the West Bank and Gaza and said the controversial tunnel would remain open.
U.S. President Bill Clinton then invited Netanyahu and Arafat to Washington for an emergency summit to try to defuse tensions threatening the U.S.-brokered peace process.
Netanyahu was elected prime minister last May after a campaign that promised to make Israelis secure after a wave of suicide bombings by Moslem militants but left much of the world nervous.

Drawing international condemnation, he has kept to a pledge to expand Jewish settlement in the West Bank; his defence minister has approved the construction of thousands of new homes in existing communities.

The right-wing leader of the Likud party roared from 20 percentage points back to overtake Prime Minister Shimon Peres, warning relentlessly that the Labour Party chief was endangering Israel in his pursuit of Middle East peace.

Only last November, the 46-year-old Netanyahu was accused of fostering the extremism that triggered the assassination of prime minister Yitzhak Rabin. At Rabin's funeral, his widow Leah Rabin would not look Netanyahu in the face.

But Islamic suicide bombers that killed 59 people this year restored an audience for the message that Israel was in danger from peace talks that could return the Golan Heights to Syria and create a Palestinian state.
Educated in the United States in business and architecture and a master of its political style, Netanyahu pounded away in television sound bytes on the theme of Peres's weakness.
Three days before the election Netanyahu got his one chance to debate Peres. The Likud leader used the word "fear" 11 times in the 30-minute showdown.
Since taking office, Netanyahu has tried to project a U.S. presidential image, travelling on state business with his third wife Sarah.
The firing several months ago of the family nanny, amid allegations that Sarah is a taskmaster, kept Israeli tabloids busy for days.

Netanyahu is known as "Bibi" (pronounced bee bee) by friend and foe alike. Netanyahu got the name, he said, "because I had a cousin who was Benjamin B. -- an older cousin. He was B.B. He was the big B.B...I was the small B.B."
Born in Tel Aviv to an eminent historian, he was in an elite army unit from 1967 to 1972. He was shot leading commandos disguised as workers onto a commandeered Sabena airliner in 1972.

In the mid-1970s he met Moshe Arens, a Likud parliamentarian who became his mentor. He was the Likud government's champion of the airwaves in the 1991 Gulf War and later that year at Israel's first talks with its Arab enemies.
After Rabin defeated Likud leader Yitzhak Shamir in the 1992 Israeli election, Netanyahu was chosen new party leader and orchestrated its return to power.
